items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in CCG lexicon parser (fromstring) on wide bracket bodies and operator chains
items.summary:
SummaryThe public CCG lexicon parser nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring parses caller-influenced lexicon text with two pure-Python loops whose cost is quadratic in the input width. A service that parses an untrusted CCG lexicon string can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by a few-megabyte input, starving the request worker. No authentication or user interaction is required.Root CausematchBrackets consumes a bracket body one character at a time with inside = inside + rest[0]; rest = rest[1:]. The rest = rest[1:] tail re-slice copies the entire remaining string on every iteration, so a flat bracket body costs O(n^2). augParseCategory drives a while rest != "": operator loop that re-copies the regular-expression match tail (rest = app[3]) once per operator, which is also O(n^2) over a long operator chain. The parser carries a recursion-depth guard (MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500) that raises on deeply nested categories, but both quadratic loops run on flat input whose nesting depth stays at zero, so that guard never fires. No bound is applied to line length or category width before the text reaches these loops.Affected functions:- nltk.ccg.lexicon.matchBrackets       (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:149-172; tail re-slice at line 168)- nltk.ccg.lexicon.augParseCategory    (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:223-268; APP_RE tail re-copy at line 250)Public entry point: nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:271), also re-exported as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring.ImpactAn attacker who can influence the CCG lexicon string parsed by an application causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The vulnerable path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with attacker-chosen input size, a few-megabyte payload costs tens of seconds per core, and a small number of concurrent requests can exhaust worker threads. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only; it does not wrap these pure-Python slicing loops, so it provides no protection here.Proof of ConceptEnvironment: nltk 3.10.3, regex 2026.9.10, CPython. Run the parser on the shipped public API.import nltk.ccg.lexicon as L# Vector A: flat bracket body -> matchBrackets tail re-slice is O(n^2)n = 400000lex_a = ":- S
w => (" + "a" * n + ")
"# Vector B: long operator chain -> augParseCategory tail re-copy is O(n^2)m = 32000lex_b = ":- a
w => " + "a" + "/a" * m + "
"import timefor name, s in (("A", lex_a), ("B", lex_b)):    t = time.perf_counter()    try:        L.fromstring(s)    except Exception:        pass  # downstream parse error is irrelevant; the CPU is already burned    print(name, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")Negative control (":- a
w => (a/a)"):   ~0.00007 sVector A (matchBrackets, flat body):     n=50k 0.078s | 100k 0.260s | 200k 1.046s | 400k 2.083s   (~4x per doubling => O(n^2))Vector B (augParseCategory, operators):  m=4k 0.078s | 8k 0.215s | 16k 0.485s | 32k 1.329s        (super-linear)Attack ChainExposure: An application calls the public nltk.ccg.lexicon.fromstring(lex_str) (also reachable as nltk.ccg.chart.fromstring) on lexicon text the attacker can influence.Control: The attacker fully controls the body width (a run of characters inside one bracket) and the operator-chain length; neither is capped by fromstring.Path: fromstring splits input into lines and routes each category through nextCategory, which dispatches to matchBrackets (Vector A) or into the augParseCategory operator loop (Vector B).Guard: The only relevant guard is the MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500 recursion-depth check. On flat input the recursion depth is zero, so if _depth > max_depth is never reached; the width loops run unbounded.Primitive: The tail re-slice rest = rest[1:] and tail re-copy rest = app[3] execute a quadratic number of string copies.Result: Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a few-megabyte lexicon costs tens of seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the parsing thread.Bypass EvidenceThe one protection present on this path is the recursion-depth guard MAX_PARSE_DEPTH = 500 (nltk/ccg/lexicon.py:22), checked at lexicon.py:153 and lexicon.py:228. It defends only against nesting depth and raises a bounded ValueError for deeply nested categories. The quadratic payloads here are flat: a single bracket body or a single operator run has nesting depth zero to one, so the depth check provably never fires while the width loops consume quadratic time. This was confirmed by running the shipped parser: the payloads complete without a ValueError or a regex TimeoutError while consuming quadratic CPU (Vector A shows a clean 4x cost per input doubling). A repository search finds no line-length or category-width cap anywhere on the fromstring path; the regex source-length limit bounds regex patterns, not lexicon text. The strongest disproof attempt (that CPython in-place string concatenation makes Vector A linear)

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in Tree.chomsky_normal_form right-factor binarization via list.pop(0)
items.summary: SummaryTree.chomsky_normal_form() binarizes a parse tree and defaults to right factoring. For a node with N children the right-factor branch repeatedly removes the first element of a working list with list.pop(0), which shifts all remaining elements each time, so binarizing one wide node costs O(N^2). An application that converts an attacker-supplied treebank tree to Chomsky Normal Form can be forced into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU by one wide flat tree. No authentication or user interaction is required.Root CauseIn the default right-factor branch the transform executes curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode] inside a loop over the N children of a node. list.pop(0) is O(len) because it shifts every remaining element down by one; performed N-2 times over a shrinking length-N list this sums to O(N^2). The left-factor branch instead uses nodeCopy.pop() (removing the last element), which is O(1) and linear overall, so the two branches differ only by this front-versus-back removal. No cap is placed on the child count of a node, and the public Tree.fromstring parser accepts an arbitrarily wide bracketed tree.Affected function:- nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/transforms.py; right-factor sink at line 168, O(1) left control at line 179)Public entry points: nltk.tree.Tree.chomsky_normal_form (nltk/tree/tree.py:455, default factor="right"); nltk.tree.Tree.fromstring (nltk/tree/tree.py:592).ImpactAn attacker who can influence the tree that an application normalizes to Chomsky Normal Form causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost grows quadratically with the attacker-chosen child count, roughly 1.5 MB of treebank input costs about 14 seconds on one core and scales as N^2 above that. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not wrap this pure-Python list loop.Proof of ConceptEnvironment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Drive the public transform on a wide flat tree.import timefrom nltk.tree import Treefor N in (80000, 160000, 320000):    s = "(S " + "(A a)" * N + ")"    t = Tree.fromstring(s)    start = time.perf_counter()    t.chomsky_normal_form()          # default factor="right"    print("right", N, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3), "s")right (default):  N=80000 1.972s | N=160000 5.004s (2.54x) | N=320000 14.518s (2.90x)   -> super-linearleft  (control):  N=80000 1.399s | N=160000 2.731s (1.95x) | N=320000  5.379s (1.97x)   -> linearAttack ChainExposure: An application parses an attacker-influenced treebank string with the public Tree.fromstring and normalizes it with Tree.chomsky_normal_form().Control: The attacker controls the number of children of a node (a wide flat tree such as (S (A a)(A a)...(A a))); no child-count cap exists in fromstring or the transform.Path: Tree.chomsky_normal_form delegates to nltk.tree.transforms.chomsky_normal_form with the default factor="right".Guard: None. There is no width bound on the loop, and the regex match timeout does not wrap this pure-Python list operation.Primitive: curNode[0:] = [nodeCopy.pop(0), newNode] performs an O(N) front shift on each of N iterations.Result: O(N^2) single-core CPU exhaustion; roughly 1.5 MB of input costs about 14 seconds and scales quadratically, blocking the processing thread.Bypass EvidenceThere is no guard to bypass on this path: neither Tree.fromstring nor chomsky_normal_form caps the child count, and the regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps only regex matching, not this list loop. The finding was confirmed by fresh timing that isolates the cause: the right-factor default and the left-factor branch build the identical bounded head strings and copy the node once, so the only differing term is pop(0) versus pop(). The measured right-versus-left divergence grows with N (right rises toward a 4x per-doubling ratio while left holds near 2x), which proves a quadratic component beyond the shared linear costs. A relevant corroboration is that the inverse transform un_chomsky_normal_form was already rewritten to a single linear pass to remove exactly this quadratic class (see the comment at nltk/tree/transforms.py:195-201), while the forward default path retained the pop(0) idiom. The strongest disproof attempt (that the head-string join dominates and is linear) fails because that join is bounded and present in both branches and therefore cannot explain the branch-dependent quadratic growth.Affected VersionsEcosystem: PyPI (pip)Package: nltkConfirmed affected range: <= 3.10.3Latest release checked: 3.10.3 (PyPI, https://pypi.org/pypi/nltk/json)Fix status: 3.10.4The right-factor pop(0) idiom ships in every release carrying this transform and is present in the current latest published release, 3.10.3. The lower boundary was not bisected, so the introducing version is left open.Suggested FixRewri

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Quadratic-time CPU denial of service in ConllCorpusReader SRL instance builder via nested span rescan
items.summary: SummaryConllCorpusReader.srl_instances() builds semantic-role-labeling instances from a CoNLL corpus block. For a sentence block with P predicates and P span columns, the instance builder rescans every span column (and every span within it) once per predicate while searching for each predicate's head, giving O(P^2 * R) work. A single well-formed block that places the head span in the last column forces the full scan on every predicate, so an application that reads an attacker-supplied CoNLL SRL corpus can be driven into tens of seconds of single-threaded CPU. No authentication or user interaction is required.Root Cause_get_srl_instances iterates over the P predicates of a block; for each predicate it scans every span list and every span within it, using an inner break that stops only when a span tagged V or C-V containing the predicate word is found. When the sole head span is placed in the last span column, no earlier column matches, so the for ... else: continue construct traverses every span of every earlier column before matching. Over P predicates each scanning up to P columns of R spans, the cost is O(P^2 * R). The block is read whole with no size cap, and the grid-consistency check enforces only uniform column count, not a bound on P, R, or total work.Affected function:- nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader._get_srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:394-424; nested rescan at lines 405-419)Public entry point: nltk.corpus.reader.conll.ConllCorpusReader.srl_instances (nltk/corpus/reader/conll.py:158-169).ImpactAn attacker who can supply a CoNLL corpus that an application loads and iterates with srl_instances() causes sustained single-threaded CPU consumption (availability loss). The path is network-reachable through any corpus-ingestion surface (AV:N) and needs no privileges or user interaction (PR:N, UI:N). Because the cost is super-linear in attacker-chosen predicate and column counts, a roughly 1 MB crafted corpus pins a core for tens of seconds and a few megabytes reaches minutes. Confidentiality and integrity are not affected. The NLTK regular-expression wall-clock timeout wraps regex matching only and does not cover this pure-Python nested loop over the parsed grid. Exploitation requires the application to use the SRL-specific API on untrusted CoNLL data with words, pos, tree, and srl columns; a deployment that never calls srl_instances() is unaffected.Proof of ConceptEnvironment: nltk 3.10.3, CPython. Stage a crafted CoNLL corpus under an authorized data root and iterate srl_instances().Corpus construction: one blank-line-delimited block with P predicate rows and P SRL span columns, the sole "V" head span in the last column.import time, os, tempfilefrom nltk.corpus.reader.conll import ConllCorpusReaderdef build_block(n):    # n predicates, n SRL columns; the single V head placed in the last column    # (columns: words pos tree srl...): emit n predicate rows and n SRL span    # columns, with the single "V" head span placed in the final column.    ...for n in (40, 80, 160, 320):    root = tempfile.mkdtemp()    open(os.path.join(root, "c.conll"), "w").write(build_block(n))    r = ConllCorpusReader(root, ["c.conll"], ("words", "pos", "tree", "srl"))    t = time.perf_counter()    list(r.srl_instances())    print(n, round(time.perf_counter() - t, 3), "s")Negative control (single predicate): n=40 -> 1.88 ms ; n=320 -> 4.45 ms      (flat)Attack (P=R=n):  n=40 -> 0.022s (10 KB) | n=80 -> 0.148s (39 KB) | n=160 -> 1.164s (156 KB) | n=320 -> 10.002s (619 KB)The attack timing rises about 8x per doubling of n while the file grows only about 4x, confirming super-linear cost driven by attacker-chosen predicate and column count; the single-predicate control stays in the millisecond range.Attack ChainExposure: An application loads an attacker-supplied CoNLL corpus (columns include srl) and iterates it with the public ConllCorpusReader(...).srl_instances().Control: The attacker controls the predicate count P, the span-column count, and the placement of the single head span; the block is read whole with no size cap.Path: srl_instances() calls _get_srl_instances, which pairs each predicate against the span columns via a doubly-nested scan.Guard: The inner break on the first matching V or C-V head is defeated by placing the sole head span in the last column, so every earlier column is scanned in full. The path-containment sandbox bounds where files load, not how much work a block costs.Primitive: The nested rescan performs O(P^2 * R) span comparisons with no work cap or timeout.Result: Sustained single-core CPU exhaustion; a roughly 1 MB corpus costs tens of seconds and scales super-linearly, blocking the processing thread.Bypass EvidenceThe only short-circuit on this path is the inner break that fires when a predicate's V or C-V head span is found.
